title: Ἄτη
about: The Achaeans are glad that Achilles has given up his wrath. Agamemnon answers from where he sits, without rising: in such an uproar nobody can hear or speak, so let them listen. He says he is not to blame for the quarrel; Zeus, Fate and the Erinys threw bewilderment on him in the assembly, and he tells how the goddess Ate once bewildered even Zeus. Hera made Zeus swear that the child born that day of his blood would rule, and then brought the child of Sthenelus’ wife into the world early, so that Eurystheus ruled over Heracles. Zeus flung Ate from Olympus, and she has lived among men ever since. Agamemnon is ready to make amends with the promised gifts and urges Achilles to rouse the army. Achilles answers briefly: give the gifts or keep them, as you like; the fighting cannot wait.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἐχάρησαν ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
μῆνιν ἀπειπόντος μεγαθύμου Πηλεΐωνος.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they rejoiced, the well-greaved Achaeans,
at the great-hearted son of Peleus renouncing his wrath.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the well-greaved Achaeans rejoiced that the great-hearted son of Peleus was renouncing his wrath.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the formula that closes a speech, here Achilles’ speech at the end of the previous part. οἳ δ’ ἐχάρησαν has the pronoun οἵ, ‘they’. μῆνιν ἀπειπόντος … Πηλεΐωνος is a genitive absolute: ἀπειπόντος is the aorist participle of ἀπεῖπον ‘renounce’, with μῆνιν ‘wrath’ as its object, and Πηλεΐωνος ‘son of Peleus’ (Achilles) is its subject. ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’ and μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ are stock epithets, translated every time.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
αὐτόθεν ἐξ ἕδρης, οὐδ’ ἐν μέσσοισιν ἀναστάς·
sentences.l:
And among them spoke also the lord of men, Agamemnon,
right there from his seat, not standing up in their midst:
sentences.i: And Agamemnon, lord of men, also spoke among them, right there from his seat, without standing up in their midst:
sentences.n: Agamemnon speaks from his seat: αὐτόθεν ἐξ ἕδρης ‘from that very spot, from his seat’, and οὐδ’ ἐν μέσσοισιν ἀναστάς ‘not having stood up in the midst’. Elsewhere a speaker rises and steps into the middle of the assembly (στὰς ἐν μέσσοισιν, 7.384); the next lines tell why Agamemnon does not. μετέειπεν is ‘spoke among’, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock title of Agamemnon. The edition prints no stop at the end of line 76.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἥρωες Δαναοὶ θεράποντες Ἄρηος
ἑσταότος μὲν καλὸν ἀκούειν, οὐδὲ ἔοικεν
ὑββάλλειν· χαλεπὸν γὰρ ἐπισταμένῳ περ ἐόντι.
sentences.l:
“O friends, heroes, Danaans, attendants of Ares,
to listen to one who stands it is good, and it is not fitting
to break in; for it is hard, even for one who is skilled.
sentences.i: “Friends, Danaan heroes, attendants of Ares: it is good to listen to a man when he stands to speak, and it is not fitting to break in; for that is hard, even for one who is skilled.
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s speech begins with a plea for quiet. ἑσταότος is the genitive of the perfect participle of ἵστημι (Attic ἑστηκότος), ‘of one who stands’, the object of ἀκούειν ‘to listen to’. ὑββάλλειν is ὑποβάλλειν with the o lost and the π made β, ‘throw in under’; ‘break in’ is the usual understanding of it, but the sense is not certain. ἐπισταμένῳ περ ἐόντι ‘even for one who is skilled’ does not say skilled at what. ἥρωες Δαναοὶ θεράποντες Ἄρηος is a stock address.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρῶν δ’ ἐν πολλῷ ὁμάδῳ πῶς κέν τις ἀκούσαι
ἢ εἴποι; βλάβεται δὲ λιγύς περ ἐὼν ἀγορητής.
sentences.l:
But amid the great din of men how could anyone listen
or speak? The speaker is hindered, clear-voiced though he be.
sentences.i: But in the great din of men, how could anyone hear or speak? Even a clear-voiced speaker is hindered.
sentences.n: A rhetorical question: in the uproar of a crowd nobody can listen or speak. ἀκούσαι and εἴποι are aorist optatives with κέν, a potential, ‘how could anyone …?’. ὁμάδῳ is ‘din, uproar’. βλάβεται is a middle or passive form of βλάπτω ‘hinder, harm’. λιγύς ‘clear-voiced’ and ἀγορητής ‘speaker’ are the house renderings, and περ ἐών ‘though he is’ makes the point that even the best voice fails in a din.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδῃ μὲν ἐγὼν ἐνδείξομαι· αὐτὰρ οἱ ἄλλοι
σύνθεσθ’ Ἀργεῖοι, μῦθόν τ’ εὖ γνῶτε ἕκαστος.
sentences.l:
To Peleus’-son, for my part, I shall make it plain; but you others,
attend, Argives, and well mark the speech, each one.
sentences.i: I shall make it plain to the son of Peleus; but the rest of you, Argives, attend, and each of you mark well what I say.
sentences.n: μέν … αὐτάρ sets Achilles against ‘the others’ (οἱ ἄλλοι). Πηλεΐδῃ is the dative of Πηλεΐδης, ‘Peleus’-son’, and ἐνδείξομαι is the future middle of ἐνδείκνυμι ‘point out, make plain’. σύνθεσθ’ is the aorist imperative middle of συντίθημι, which in the middle can mean ‘take in, attend to’. γνῶτε is the aorist imperative of γιγνώσκω, ‘get to know, understand’. Ἀργεῖοι is simply the army, one of the poet’s three names for it.

sentences.t:
πολλάκι δή μοι τοῦτον Ἀχαιοὶ μῦθον ἔειπον
καί τέ με νεικείεσκον· ἐγὼ δ’ οὐκ αἴτιός εἰμι,
sentences.l:
Often indeed the Achaeans have spoken this word to me
and used to rebuke me; but I am not to blame,
sentences.i: Often the Achaeans have said this to me, and used to rebuke me for it; but I am not to blame,
sentences.n: τοῦτον … μῦθον ‘this word’ is the charge Agamemnon is about to answer, that he is to blame. πολλάκι is the poetic form of πολλάκις ‘often’. νεικείεσκον is an iterative past, with the suffix -εσκ- that marks a repeated action: ‘they used to rebuke’. ἐγὼ δ’ οὐκ αἴτιός εἰμι ‘but I am not to blame’ opens the defence; αἴτιος is the adjective ‘responsible, to blame’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς καὶ Μοῖρα καὶ ἠεροφοῖτις Ἐρινύς,
οἵ τέ μοι εἰν ἀγορῇ φρεσὶν ἔμβαλον ἄγριον ἄτην,
ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ Ἀχιλλῆος γέρας αὐτὸς ἀπηύρων.
sentences.l:
but Zeus and Portion and the mist-walking Erinys,
who in the assembly cast into my wits a savage bewilderment,
on that day when I myself took away Achilles’ prize.
sentences.i: but Zeus and Fate and the Erinys who walks in the mist, who in the assembly cast a savage bewilderment into my mind on the day when I myself took away Achilles’ prize.
sentences.n: Three powers are named as the cause: Zeus, Μοῖρα (‘Portion’, Fate, personified) and the Erinys, a spirit of vengeance; ἠεροφοῖτις ‘mist-walking’ is the epithet she has at 9.571. ἄτη ‘bewilderment’ is a clouding of the wits sent from outside; the goddess Ἄτη appears at 91. ἔμβαλον is ‘cast into’. The day is that of the quarrel in Book 1: ἀπηύρων is ‘I took away’, the verb used of seizing a prize, and γέρας is ‘prize of honour’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τί κεν ῥέξαιμι; θεὸς διὰ πάντα τελευτᾷ.
sentences.l: But what could I do? A god brings all things to fulfilment.
sentences.i: But what could I do? A god brings everything to its end.
sentences.n: τί κεν ῥέξαιμι; is a question with the potential optative, ‘what could I do?’, ῥέξαιμι being the aorist optative of ῥέζω ‘do’. τελευτᾷ is the contracted present of τελευτάω ‘bring to an end, accomplish’, and διὰ πάντα ‘through all things’ makes the god’s power complete. θεός has no article, so it is ‘a god’ or ‘god’ in general. The sentence is Agamemnon’s answer to his own question, and it is also his defence.

sentences.t:
πρέσβα Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἄτη, ἣ πάντας ἀᾶται,
οὐλομένη·
sentences.l:
August Ate, Zeus’s daughter, who bewilders all,
the ruinous one:
sentences.i: August Ate, Zeus’s daughter, who bewilders everyone, the ruinous one:
sentences.n: Ate (Ἄτη) is the personified force of ἄτη ‘bewilderment’, which Agamemnon has just named; he now describes her. πρέσβα is a title of honour, ‘august’ (it can also mean ‘eldest’; both suit a daughter of Zeus). ἀᾶται is a present of ἀάω, the verb that stands behind her name: ‘she bewilders’. οὐλομένη ‘the ruinous one’ is the word used of the wrath at 1.2. πάντας ‘all’ is the object of ἀᾶται. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the final η of Ἄτη stands in hiatus before ἣ, at the comma, and must be counted long.

sentences.t:
τῇ μέν θ’ ἁπαλοὶ πόδες· οὐ γὰρ ἐπ’ οὔδει
πίλναται, ἀλλ’ ἄρα ἥ γε κατ’ ἀνδρῶν κράατα βαίνει
βλάπτουσ’ ἀνθρώπους·
sentences.i: Her feet are tender; for she does not tread on the ground, but walks over the heads of men, harming people;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 92. τῇ is the dative used for possession, ‘to her are tender feet’, and μέν θ’ adds a general statement. The reason follows with γάρ: she does not ‘draw near’ (πίλναται, a poetic verb) to the ground, but goes over men’s heads; κράατα is the epic plural of the word for ‘head’, like κάρη. βλάπτουσ’ is the participle of βλάπτω ‘harm’, the verb of βλάβεται at 82.

sentences.t: κατὰ δ’ οὖν ἕτερόν γε πέδησε.
sentences.l: and down she fettered another, at any rate.
sentences.i: and at any rate she has caught another in her fetters.
sentences.n: This unit is the last part of line 94. κατὰ … πέδησε is tmesis, the preposition set apart from its verb: καταπεδάω ‘fetter down’, in the aorist, said of a general fact (‘she has fettered’). δ’ οὖν is ‘and at any rate’, and ἕτερον ‘another’ leads into the example of Zeus in the next sentence. The verb πεδάω is the one that binds a man with a fetter (πέδη), so Ate is imagined as trapping her victims.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ δή νύ ποτε Ζεὺς ἄσατο, τόν περ ἄριστον
ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ θεῶν φασ’ ἔμμεναι· ἀλλ’ ἄρα καὶ τὸν
Ἥρη θῆλυς ἐοῦσα δολοφροσύνῃς ἀπάτησεν,
sentences.l:
For indeed once Zeus too was bewildered, he whom they say to be the best
of men and gods; but even him
Hera, being female, deceived by trickery,
sentences.i: For once even Zeus was bewildered, though they say he is the best of men and gods; but even him Hera, though only a female, deceived by trickery,
sentences.n: καὶ γὰρ δή νύ ποτε ‘for indeed once’ begins the example. ἄσατο is the aorist of ἀάω, ‘was bewildered’, from the same root as ἄτη. τόν περ ἄριστον … φασ’ ἔμμεναι is ‘the very one they say is best’: φασ’ is φασί ‘they say’, and ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί. θῆλυς ἐοῦσα ‘being female’ is contemptuous and sharpens the surprise. δολοφροσύνῃς ‘by trickery’ (δόλος ‘trick’ + φρήν ‘mind’) has an unusual epic ending; it is read as a dative singular, instrumental in sense.

sentences.t:
ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ ἔμελλε βίην Ἡρακληείην
Ἀλκμήνη τέξεσθαι ἐϋστεφάνῳ ἐνὶ Θήβῃ.
sentences.l:
on that day when she was about to bear the might of Heracles,
Alcmene, in fair-crowned Thebe.
sentences.i: on the day when Alcmene was about to bear the might of Heracles in fair-crowned Thebe.
sentences.n: ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ ‘on the day when’ repeats the words of line 89 and ties the two bewilderments together. ἔμελλε with the future infinitive τέξεσθαι (from τίκτω ‘bear’) means ‘was about to bear’. βίην Ἡρακληείην ‘the might of Heracles’ is a periphrasis for the hero himself, and Ἡρακληείην is an adjective formed on his name. Θήβῃ is the dative of Θήβη, Thebe; ἐϋστεφάνῳ is ‘fair-crowned’, as of Mycene, probably the walls as a crown, though the picture is not certain.

sentences.t: ἤτοι ὅ γ’ εὐχόμενος μετέφη πάντεσσι θεοῖσι·
sentences.l: He indeed, boasting, spoke among all the gods:
sentences.i: He spoke among all the gods, boasting:
sentences.n: Zeus is the ὅ γ’ of the line: ‘he indeed’ takes up Zeus as the subject again after the sentence about Hera. εὐχόμενος is the participle of εὔχομαι, a verb that in Homer covers ‘pray’, ‘vow’ and ‘boast’; here, with the proud announcement that follows, it is ‘boasting’. μετέφη ‘spoke among’ is the same sense as μετέειπεν of Agamemnon at 76 and introduces Zeus’s words, which Agamemnon quotes inside his own speech; they are marked with single quotation marks.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ πάντές τε θεοὶ πᾶσαί τε θέαιναι,
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀνώγει.
sentences.l:
‘Hear me, all gods and all goddesses,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: ‘Hear me, all you gods and all you goddesses, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: κέκλυτέ μευ ‘hear me’ is the reduplicated imperative of κλύω with the genitive μευ, the usual call for attention at an assembly. Line 101 is found word for word elsewhere; in 102 the verb is ἀνώγει (from ἄνωγα ‘I bid’), where the same line elsewhere has κελεύει, ‘bids’. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive: ‘so that I may say’. θυμός ‘heart’ is the seat of the urge to speak, and θέαιναι is the feminine of θεός, ‘goddesses’.
sentences.mark: Zeus speaks, as Agamemnon tells it

sentences.t:
σήμερον ἄνδρα φόως δὲ μογοστόκος Εἰλείθυια
ἐκφανεῖ, ὃς πάντεσσι περικτιόνεσσιν ἀνάξει,
τῶν ἀνδρῶν γενεῆς οἵ θ’ αἵματος ἐξ ἐμεῦ εἰσί.
sentences.l:
Today into the light the travail-bringing Eileithyia
will bring a man, who will be lord over all the dwellers-around,
of the men of the lineage who are of blood from me.’
sentences.i: Today Eileithyia, goddess of the travail of birth, will bring a man into the light, one who will rule over all his neighbours, of the men of my own lineage, those of my blood.’
sentences.n: σήμερον ‘today’ is the day of Heracles’ birth in the tale. φόως δέ is ‘into the light’, with the suffix -δε of motion; μογοστόκος Εἰλείθυια is the goddess of childbirth. ἐκφανεῖ and ἀνάξει are futures of ἐκφαίνω ‘bring to light’ and ἀνάσσω ‘be lord’, the latter with the dative περικτιόνεσσιν ‘dwellers-around, neighbours’. τῶν ἀνδρῶν γενεῆς is partitive, ‘of the men of the lineage’. Zeus names no child, and Hera will use that gap.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ δολοφρονέουσα προσηύδα πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.l: And to him, with guile in her mind, spoke lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then lady Hera, with guile in her mind, spoke to him:
sentences.n: This whole line introduces Hera’s reply to Zeus, and it is the same line as 14.300, where she also deceives him. δολοφρονέουσα ‘with guile in her mind’ is the participle of δολοφρονέω (δόλος ‘trick’ + φρήν ‘mind’), a promise of the trick she is about to play; τὸν δέ ‘to him’ is Zeus, and προσηύδα is ‘spoke to’. The speech is quoted inside Agamemnon’s tale, so it takes single quotation marks from the next line.

sentences.t: ψευστήσεις, οὐδ’ αὖτε τέλος μύθῳ ἐπιθήσεις.
sentences.l: ‘You will play false, and again you will not put fulfilment on the word.
sentences.i: ‘You will play false, and once again you will not bring your word to fulfilment.
sentences.n: Hera begins with a taunt. ψευστήσεις is a future of a rare verb from the family of ψεύδομαι ‘lie’, so ‘you will play false’; the sense is rebuilt from that root. οὐδ’ αὖτε τέλος μύθῳ ἐπιθήσεις is ‘nor again will you put fulfilment on the word’: τέλος is the ‘end, fulfilment’, ἐπιθήσεις the future of ἐπιτίθημι ‘put on’. She is saying that Zeus’s announcement will not come true, to provoke him into an oath.
sentences.mark: Hera speaks, as Agamemnon tells it

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἄγε νῦν μοι ὄμοσσον Ὀλύμπιε καρτερὸν ὅρκον,
sentences.l: But come now, swear to me, Olympian, a mighty oath,
sentences.i: But come now, swear me a solemn oath, Olympian:
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγε νῦν is a fixed way of urging, ‘but come now’. ὄμοσσον is the aorist imperative of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’, with the doubled σ that the epic allows; μοι is ‘to me’. Ὀλύμπιε is the vocative of Ὀλύμπιος, here Zeus. καρτερὸν ὅρκον is the house ‘mighty oath’ in the literal layer. The oath asked for is the means by which Hera traps him, and its content is given in the next unit, after ἦ μέν.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν τὸν πάντεσσι περικτιόνεσσιν ἀνάξειν
ὅς κεν ἐπ’ ἤματι τῷδε πέσῃ μετὰ ποσσὶ γυναικὸς
τῶν ἀνδρῶν οἳ σῆς ἐξ αἵματός εἰσι γενέθλης.
sentences.l:
that truly over all the dwellers-around will be lord
the man who on this day shall fall between the feet of a woman,
of the men who are of the blood of your stock.’
sentences.i: that the man who falls between a woman’s feet on this day, one of the men who are of your blood and stock, will truly be lord over all his neighbours.’
sentences.n: ἦ μέν ‘truly’ introduces the content of an oath, followed by the future infinitive ἀνάξειν ‘will be lord’ (the future of 104). ὅς κεν … πέσῃ is ‘whoever shall fall’ (aorist subjunctive with κε), and ‘to fall between a woman’s feet’ is a picture of being born. Zeus had spoken of one child; Hera’s words fit any descendant of his born that day, and that is the trap. σῆς ἐξ αἵματός … γενέθλης is ‘of the blood of your stock’; γενέθλη is ‘stock, family’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατο· Ζεὺς δ’ οὔ τι δολοφροσύνην ἐνόησεν,
ἀλλ’ ὄμοσεν μέγαν ὅρκον, ἔπειτα δὲ πολλὸν ἀάσθη.
sentences.l:
So she spoke; but Zeus did not at all perceive the trickery,
but swore a great oath, and then was greatly bewildered.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Zeus did not at all see through the trickery, but swore a great oath, and was then deeply bewildered.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο closes Hera’s speech, and from here Agamemnon tells the story in his own voice again. δολοφροσύνην ‘trickery’ is the noun of 97, built on the same words as δολοφρονέουσα. ἐνόησεν is the aorist of νοέω, ‘perceive, grasp’. ἀάσθη is the aorist passive of ἀάω, ‘was bewildered’, the same verb as ἄσατο at 95; πολλόν is an adverb, ‘greatly’. ἔπειτα δέ ‘and then’ shows the order: the oath first, then the blindness. μέγαν ὅρκον is ‘a great oath’.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη δ’ ἀΐξασα λίπεν ῥίον Οὐλύμποιο,
καρπαλίμως δ’ ἵκετ’ Ἄργος Ἀχαιικόν, ἔνθ’ ἄρα ᾔδη
ἰφθίμην ἄλοχον Σθενέλου Περσηϊάδαο.
sentences.l:
and Hera, darting, left the crag of Olympus,
and swiftly came to Achaean Argos, where she knew
the mighty wife of Sthenelus, Perseus’-son,
sentences.i: and Hera darted off and left the crag of Olympus, and swiftly came to Achaean Argos, where she knew the mighty wife of Sthenelus, the son of Perseus,
sentences.n: ἀΐξασα ‘darting’ is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω, and ῥίον Οὐλύμποιο ‘the crag of Olympus’ has the epic genitive -οιο. καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’. Ἄργος Ἀχαιικόν is ‘Achaean Argos’, the home of Sthenelus, Perseus’ son, whose line will produce Eurystheus; his wife is not named. ᾔδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα, used as a past, ‘she knew’. ἰφθίμην ‘mighty’ is the stock epithet of a wife, and Περσηϊάδαο is a patronymic, ‘son of Perseus’, with the epic ending -αο.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἐκύει φίλον υἱόν, ὃ δ’ ἕβδομος ἑστήκει μείς·
sentences.l: and she was carrying a dear son, and the seventh month was standing;
sentences.i: She was carrying a dear son, and it was the seventh month;
sentences.n: ἐκύει is the imperfect of κυέω, ‘be pregnant with’, so ‘she was carrying’. μείς is the epic and Ionic form of μήν ‘month’, and ἕβδομος ἑστήκει μείς is ‘the seventh month was standing’: ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, which has the sense of an imperfect, ‘was standing’, and the idiom is a month that is in progress. The child is not named until line 123: it is Eurystheus, and Hera’s plan is to hasten his birth.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄγαγε πρὸ φόως δὲ καὶ ἠλιτόμηνον ἐόντα,
Ἀλκμήνης δ’ ἀπέπαυσε τόκον, σχέθε δ’ Εἰλειθυίας.
sentences.l:
and she led him out into the light, though he was one who had missed his months,
and from Alcmene she stopped the birth, and held back the Eileithyiae.
sentences.i: and she brought him out into the light, though he was born before his time, and stopped Alcmene’s labour and held back the Eileithyiae.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἄγαγε is tmesis of ἐξήγαγε ‘led out’, and φόως δέ is ‘into the light’, as at 103. ἠλιτόμηνον is a compound on μήν ‘month’ whose first part is usually linked to ἀλιτεῖν ‘miss, err’, so ‘one who has missed his months’; its formation is debated, and the seventh month fixes the sense as ‘premature’. Ἀλκμήνης … τόκον is ‘Alcmene’s delivery’. σχέθε is the aorist of ἔχω, ‘held back’, and Εἰλειθυίας is the accusative plural, the goddesses of childbirth, as at 11.270.

sentences.t: αὐτὴ δ’ ἀγγελέουσα Δία Κρονίωνα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: And she herself, to tell the news, spoke to Zeus the son of Cronus:
sentences.i: And she herself, to bring him news, spoke to Zeus, the son of Cronus:
sentences.n: ἀγγελέουσα is a future participle of purpose, ‘about to tell the news, in order to tell it’ (the same word as at 8.398). αὐτή ‘herself’ means that Hera goes in person, as she did to Argos. Δία Κρονίωνα is ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’, the stock title; Κρονίων is a patronymic. προσηύδα is ‘spoke to’, and Hera’s speech to Zeus follows, quoted inside Agamemnon’s speech with single quotation marks.

sentences.t: Ζεῦ πάτερ ἀργικέραυνε ἔπος τί τοι ἐν φρεσὶ θήσω·
sentences.l: ‘Father Zeus, of the bright thunderbolt, some word to you in your wits I shall place:
sentences.i: ‘Father Zeus, of the bright thunderbolt, I shall put a word in your mind:
sentences.n: Ζεῦ πάτερ is the vocative ‘Father Zeus’. ἀργικέραυνε is the vocative of ἀργικέραυνος, from ἀργής ‘bright, white’ and κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’: ‘of the bright thunderbolt’. ἔπος τί τοι ἐν φρεσὶ θήσω is ‘I shall put some word in your wits’, the idiom of making someone lay a thing to heart; θήσω is the future of τίθημι, and τοι is the dative ‘to you’.
sentences.mark: Hera speaks to Zeus, as Agamemnon tells it

sentences.t:
ἤδη ἀνὴρ γέγον’ ἐσθλὸς ὃς Ἀργείοισιν ἀνάξει
Εὐρυσθεὺς Σθενέλοιο πάϊς Περσηϊάδαο
σὸν γένος· οὔ οἱ ἀεικὲς ἀνασσέμεν Ἀργείοισιν.
sentences.l:
Already a man has been born, a good one, who will be lord over the Argives,
Eurystheus, child of Sthenelus, Perseus’-son,
your own race; it is no unseemly thing for him to be lord over the Argives.’
sentences.i: A good man has already been born, who will rule over the Argives: Eurystheus, child of Sthenelus the son of Perseus, of your own race; it is no unseemly thing for him to rule over the Argives.’
sentences.n: ἤδη ‘already’ is Hera’s point: the child is now born. γέγον’ is the perfect of γίγνομαι, ‘has been born’. ὃς Ἀργείοισιν ἀνάξει echoes ὃς πάντεσσι περικτιόνεσσιν ἀνάξει of 104 and 109–110, so that Eurystheus seems to qualify. Σθενέλοιο has the epic ending -οιο, and πάϊς is παῖς ‘child’. σὸν γένος ‘your race’ points to Perseus, a son of Zeus (14.319–320). οὔ οἱ ἀεικὲς ἀνασσέμεν ‘it is no unseemly thing for him to be lord’: ἀνασσέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀνάσσω.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ ἄχος ὀξὺ κατὰ φρένα τύψε βαθεῖαν·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and him a sharp grief struck in his deep mind;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and sharp grief struck him in his deep mind;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so she spoke’ closes Hera’s speech. ἄχος ὀξύ is ‘sharp grief’, and τύψε is the aorist of τύπτω ‘strike’ without the augment. κατὰ φρένα βαθεῖαν is ‘in his deep mind’, with βαθεῖαν agreeing with φρένα. Zeus now sees that he has been tricked. The line begins Agamemnon’s own narration again, so there are no single quotation marks.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ εἷλ’ Ἄτην κεφαλῆς λιπαροπλοκάμοιο
χωόμενος φρεσὶν ᾗσι, καὶ ὤμοσε καρτερὸν ὅρκον
μή ποτ’ ἐς Οὔλυμπόν τε καὶ οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα
αὖτις ἐλεύσεσθαι Ἄτην, ἣ πάντας ἀᾶται.
sentences.l:
At once he seized Ate by the head, of the sleek locks,
incensed in his own wits, and swore a mighty oath
that never to Olympus and the starry sky
again would come Ate, she who bewilders all.
sentences.i: At once he seized Ate by her head of sleek locks, incensed in his own mind, and swore a solemn oath that Ate, who bewilders everyone, would never come again to Olympus and the starry sky.
sentences.n: εἷλ’ is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’, with the genitive κεφαλῆς for the part he takes hold of. λιπαροπλοκάμοιο ‘of sleek locks’ (λιπαρός ‘sleek’ + πλόκαμος ‘lock’) has the epic genitive -οιο. χωόμενος ‘incensed’ is a participle; ᾗσι is the possessive ‘his own’, to be kept apart from the relative. μή ποτ’ … ἐλεύσεσθαι, with the future infinitive, gives the content of the oath: ‘that she shall never come’. οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα is the ‘starry sky’. ἣ πάντας ἀᾶται repeats 91.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἔρριψεν ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος
χειρὶ περιστρέψας· τάχα δ’ ἵκετο ἔργ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he flung her from the starry sky,
whirling her round with his hand; and soon she came to the works of men.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and flung her from the starry sky, whirling her round with his hand; and soon she came to the works of men.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ joins the oath to the act. ἔρριψεν is the aorist of ῥίπτω ‘fling’, the verb of Hephaestus’ fall from Olympus (1.591). περιστρέψας is the aorist participle of περιστρέφω ‘whirl round’. τάχα is ‘soon’, and ἵκετο the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘came’. ἔργ’ ἀνθρώπων ‘the works of men’ means the world of human toil and affairs, where Ate does her harm; the ‘starry sky’ is the house rendering again.

sentences.t:
τὴν αἰεὶ στενάχεσχ’ ὅθ’ ἑὸν φίλον υἱὸν ὁρῷτο
ἔργον ἀεικὲς ἔχοντα ὑπ’ Εὐρυσθῆος ἀέθλων.
sentences.l:
Her he would always groan over whenever he saw his own dear son
having an unseemly task under the labours of Eurystheus.
sentences.i: He would always groan over her whenever he saw his own dear son doing unseemly work under the labours set by Eurystheus.
sentences.n: τήν is Ate, the object of the groaning. στενάχεσχ’ is στενάχεσκε, an iterative with the suffix -εσκ-, ‘he would groan’, its κ turned into χ before the rough breathing of ὅθ’. ὁρῷτο is an optative of ὁράω in a middle form, used for a repeated event, ‘whenever he saw’. φίλον υἱόν is Heracles, who is not named; ἔργον ἀεικές ‘an unseemly task’ and ἀέθλων ‘labours’ are the work Eurystheus imposed. ὑπ’ with the genitive means ‘under’.

sentences.t:
ὣς καὶ ἐγών, ὅτε δ’ αὖτε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
Ἀργείους ὀλέκεσκεν ἐπὶ πρυμνῇσι νέεσσιν,
οὐ δυνάμην λελαθέσθ’ Ἄτης ᾗ πρῶτον ἀάσθην.
sentences.l:
So too I; whenever again great Hector of the glancing helmet
was destroying the Argives at the sterns of the ships,
I could not forget Ate, by whom first I was bewildered.
sentences.i: So it was with me too: whenever great Hector of the glancing helmet was destroying the Argives at the sterns of the ships, I could not forget Ate, by whom I was first bewildered.
sentences.n: ὣς καὶ ἐγών ‘so I too’ draws the comparison with Zeus, whose grief for his son was caused by Ate. ὀλέκεσκεν is an iterative imperfect of ὀλέκω ‘destroy’, ‘whenever he was destroying’. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s stock epithet. δυνάμην is the imperfect of δύναμαι; λελαθέσθαι is a reduplicated aorist infinitive of λήθομαι, ‘forget’, with the genitive Ἄτης. ᾗ is the relative ‘by whom’, and ἀάσθην the aorist passive of ἀάω ‘I was bewildered’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἀασάμην καί μευ φρένας ἐξέλετο Ζεύς,
ἂψ ἐθέλω ἀρέσαι, δόμεναί τ’ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα·
sentences.l:
But since I was bewildered and Zeus took away my wits,
back I wish to make him content and to give unstinted ransom;
sentences.i: But since I was bewildered, and Zeus took away my wits, I wish to make him content again and to give an unstinted ransom;
sentences.n: ἀασάμην is the aorist of ἀάομαι, ‘I was bewildered’ (as at 9.116), the same root as ἄτη. φρένας ἐξέλετο is ‘took away my wits’: ἐξέλετο is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω. Line 138 is the line Agamemnon spoke in Book 9 (9.120): ἂψ ἐθέλω ἀρέσαι ‘I wish to make him content again’, with δόμεναι the epic infinitive of δίδωμι, ‘to give’. The object of ἀρέσαι, Achilles, is left unsaid. ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα is ‘unstinted ransom’, the house rendering.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὄρσευ πόλεμον δὲ καὶ ἄλλους ὄρνυθι λαούς.
sentences.l: But rouse yourself to war, and rouse the other peoples.
sentences.i: But rise to the war, and rouse the rest of the army.
sentences.n: ὄρσευ is the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, with the ending -ευ for -εο: ‘rouse yourself, get up’. πόλεμον δέ is ‘to war’, with the suffix -δε of motion towards. ὄρνυθι is the present imperative of the same verb, ‘rouse’ with an object, and ἄλλους λαούς are the other contingents of the army. Agamemnon asks Achilles both to go to battle and to bring the rest with him.

sentences.t:
δῶρα δ’ ἐγὼν ὅδε πάντα παρασχέμεν ὅσσά τοι ἐλθὼν
χθιζὸς ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν ὑπέσχετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
And the gifts, I here am ready to provide all of them, as many as to you,
having come yesterday in your huts, heavenly Odysseus promised.
sentences.i: And I am here ready to provide all the gifts that heavenly Odysseus promised you yesterday when he came to your huts.
sentences.n: δῶρα … παρασχέμεν: the infinitive stands for an offer, ‘I am here to provide’, and ὅδε ‘this man here’ is Agamemnon himself. παρασχέμεν is an epic infinitive in -μεν. ὑπέσχετο is ‘promised’, ἐλθών ‘having come’ goes with Odysseus, and χθιζός ‘yesterday’ is an adjective used as an adverb. The promise is the offer Odysseus carried to Achilles’ hut in Book 9, which Achilles then refused. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet of Odysseus.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις, ἐπίμεινον ἐπειγόμενός περ Ἄρηος,
δῶρα δέ τοι θεράποντες ἐμῆς παρὰ νηὸς ἑλόντες
οἴσουσ’, ὄφρα ἴδηαι ὅ τοι μενοεικέα δώσω.
sentences.l:
But if you wish, wait, though you are pressing on to Ares,
and for you the gifts, the attendants, having taken them from beside my ship,
will bring, so that you may see that I shall give you satisfying things.”
sentences.i: But if you wish, wait, eager though you are for battle; my attendants will take the gifts from my ship and bring them to you, so that you may see that I shall give you satisfying things.”
sentences.n: ἐπίμεινον is the aorist imperative of ἐπιμένω ‘wait’. ἐπειγόμενός περ Ἄρηος is ‘though pressing on towards Ares’, the war-god standing for war itself. θεράποντες here are ordinary attendants, not the θεράποντες Ἄρηος of line 78. οἴσουσ’ is the future οἴσουσι of φέρω ‘bring’. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive ἴδηαι gives purpose; ὅ is used for ‘that’. μενοεικέα ‘satisfying’ is the house rendering. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: This whole line is the stock introduction of a reply, and it recurs throughout the poem with the speaker’s name. ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is a present participle, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ is the aorist of πρόσφημι. πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift of foot’ has the accusative of respect: ‘swift as to the feet’. Achilles’ short reply follows, in double quotation marks again.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
δῶρα μὲν αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα παρασχέμεν, ὡς ἐπιεικές,
ἤ τ’ ἐχέμεν παρὰ σοί·
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, as for the gifts, if you wish to provide them, as is fitting, or to keep them with you;
sentences.n: The address is a stock one: Ἀτρεΐδη ‘son of Atreus’, κύδιστε ‘most glorious’, ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’. δῶρα μέν ‘as for the gifts’ is answered by νῦν δέ ‘but now’ in the next unit. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is εἰ κε ἐθέλῃς, with the epic ending -σθα of the second person; παρασχέμεν and ἐχέμεν are epic infinitives in -μεν. ὡς ἐπιεικές is ‘as is fitting’. Achilles leaves the matter of the gifts to Agamemnon: give them or keep them.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ μνησώμεθα χάρμης
αἶψα μάλ’·
sentences.l:
but now let us be mindful of the joy of battle,
very quickly;
sentences.i: but let us now be mindful of the joy of battle, and very quickly;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 148. νῦν δέ ‘but now’ answers δῶρα μέν. μνησώμεθα is the aorist subjunctive of μιμνῄσκομαι, a call to the group, ‘let us be mindful of’, with the genitive χάρμης ‘joy of battle’, the house rendering. αἶψα μάλ’ ‘very quickly’ adds urgency. The stop after μάλ’ ends the sentence, and the next unit gives the reason.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ χρὴ κλοτοπεύειν ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντας
οὐδὲ διατρίβειν· ἔτι γὰρ μέγα ἔργον ἄρεκτον·
sentences.l:
for it is not right to dawdle, being here,
nor to waste time; for still a great work is undone;
sentences.i: for we must not dawdle here, nor waste time; there is still a great work undone;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 149. κλοτοπεύειν occurs only here in Homer and its meaning is not known for certain; ‘dawdle’ is a guess from the context and from the next verb, διατρίβειν ‘wear away time, waste time’. ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντας is a participle agreeing with an unspoken ‘us’, ‘being here’. ἄρεκτον ‘undone’ is ἀ- + the root of ῥέζω ‘do’, and the ‘great work’ is the fighting.

sentences.t:
ὥς κέ τις αὖτ’ Ἀχιλῆα μετὰ πρώτοισιν ἴδηται
ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ Τρώων ὀλέκοντα φάλαγγας.
ὧδέ τις ὑμείων μεμνημένος ἀνδρὶ μαχέσθω.
sentences.l:
so that someone may again see Achilles among the foremost
with his bronze spear destroying the battle-lines of the Trojans.
Thus let each of you, being mindful, fight with a man.”
sentences.i: so that any man may see Achilles again among the foremost, destroying the battle-lines of the Trojans with his bronze spear. So let each of you keep this in mind and fight his man.”
sentences.n: ὥς κέ τις … ἴδηται is a purpose clause, with the aorist subjunctive ἴδηται: ‘so that someone may see’. αὖτ’ is αὖτε, ‘again’ or ‘in turn’. μετὰ πρώτοισιν is ‘among the foremost’, the front rank. ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ is ‘with a bronze spear’, and ὀλέκοντα ‘destroying’ is a participle agreeing with Ἀχιλῆα. μεμνημένος is the perfect participle of μιμνῄσκομαι, ‘being mindful’, as in μνησώμεθα above. ὑμείων is the epic ὑμῶν. Achilles’ speech ends here.
